name: NHS Flexibility Exercises
description: Four short NHS stretches for the neck, side and calves - gentle enough for anyone starting from a low baseline.
whoItsFor: Anyone easing back into movement, including people who haven't exercised in a while, who want a short, safe flexibility routine with no equipment.
howToRun: Do this at least twice a week; it pairs with the NHS strength and balance routines.
Build up the repetitions gradually over time, and stop if you feel pain or become unwell.
Wear loose, comfortable clothing and keep water handy.
These are general exercises, not a treatment for a specific injury or condition - see a GP or physio if something hurts.

exercises.name: Calf Stretch
exercises.reps: each side (NHS gives no hold time for this one)

name: Cleveland Clinic Everyday Flexibility Stretches
description: Five static stretches for the hips, glutes, back, hamstrings and thighs from a Cleveland Clinic exercise physiologist.
whoItsFor: Anyone wanting a short daily stretch routine for the lower body and back - no workout required beforehand.
howToRun: Do about 10 minutes of stretching, up to twice a day, depending on how tight you feel.
Start each hold at 20-30 seconds; as your mobility improves, build up to 1-2 minutes.
Stretch to the point of mild tension, never pain - stop if anything hurts.
Consistency matters more than any single session; work it into your day where you can.

exercises.name: Standing Quad Stretch
exercises.reps: 20-30s (source does not specify a side count)

exercises.name: Seated Hip Stretch
exercises.reps: 20-30s (source does not specify a side count)

credit: Christopher Travers, MS (Cleveland Clinic, Health Essentials)

name: Cleveland Clinic Dynamic Warm-Up Movements
description: Three dynamic, moving warm-up drills from a Cleveland Clinic osteopathic physician: a leg pendulum, walking lunges and hip circles.
whoItsFor: Anyone about to train who wants to move the hips and legs through their range before the main session, rather than holding a stretch cold.
howToRun: Do this right before training, not instead of your sport's own warm-up.
Keep moving throughout - don't hold any position; the aim is to move each joint through its full range.
Go through each drill at an easy pace first, then a little quicker as you warm up.
Move straight into your workout afterwards - save held (static) stretches for after you train.

exercises.name: Walking Lunge
exercises.reps: 8/leg (source gives no rep count; used as a typical dose)

exercises.name: Small Hip Circles
exercises.reps: 10 each way (source gives no rep count; used as a typical dose)

credit: Dr. Anne Rex, DO (Cleveland Clinic, Health Essentials)
sourceNote: Free Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials article (dated 29 Aug 2024), expert-reviewed by Dr. Anne Rex. No reuse terms stated. The leg-pendulum rep count (10-12 swings/leg) is exactly as given; the article names walking lunges and small hip circles as examples but gives no rep count for either, so a typical dose is used and flagged here rather than presented as the source's own number - this is the same split used for the companion static-stretch entry from the same article.

name: Cleveland Clinic Static Cool-Down Stretches
description: Five classic static stretches - hamstring, calf, triceps, quad and shoulder - from the same Cleveland Clinic article's cool-down section.
whoItsFor: Anyone finishing a workout who wants a short, held-stretch routine while the muscles are still warm.
howToRun: Do this after training, once your breathing has settled and your muscles are still warm.
Hold each stretch for 30-90 seconds, breathing deeply throughout.
This is the time for static holds - save fast, moving drills for your warm-up instead.
Ease off if a stretch becomes painful; mild tension is normal, pain is not.
credit: Dr. Anne Rex, DO (Cleveland Clinic, Health Essentials)
sourceNote: Same article and expert as x-mobility-clevelandclinic-dynamic-warmup, split by the article's own dynamic-vs-static framing: this entry is its static, post-workout half. The 30-90 second hold range and all five stretch names are exactly as given; the article does not state a per-side count for any of the five, which is reflected by leaving reps as a plain hold time rather than inventing a side count.
